projects.title: Modular Scientific Geometry & Engineering Mensuration Suite
projects.description: Industrial CAD software breaks geometric mathematics into modular, reusable function subroutines. In this project, you will construct a Modular Geometry Engineering Suite in C. The program declares function prototypes for 2D circles, 3D cylinders, and 3D spheres above main(). The cylinder volume function demonstrates modular reuse by invoking the circleArea() function directly within its calculation body.
projects.learningOutcome: Function Prototypes, Subroutine Decomposition & Modular Function Reusability
projects.exampleOutput:
Dimensions: Radius = 5.00 units, Height = 12.00 units

1. Circle Area          :    78.5398 sq units
2. Circle Circumference :    31.4159 units
3. Cylinder Volume      :   942.4778 cubic units
4. Sphere Volume        :   523.5988 cubic units
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Prototypes**: Declared above main to inform compiler of signatures.
2. **Modular Reuse**: `cylinderVolume` calls `circleArea(r) * h`.
3. **Precision**: Uses standard double-precision floating-point arithmetic.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. Prototypes establish API interfaces.
2. Definitions implement domain logic cleanly.

projects.title: High-Speed Integer Arithmetic & Stats Out-Parameter Package
projects.description: C functions cannot return multiple values directly via return statements. To overcome this limitation, systems software passes memory addresses as pointer out-parameters. In this project, you will build an Array Statistics Engine in C that computes the minimum value, maximum value, total sum, and arithmetic mean of an array, writing all 4 computed outputs back into the caller's stack frame variables via pointer out-parameters.
projects.learningOutcome: Pointer Out-Parameters, Passing Memory Addresses (&), Call Stack Modification & Defensive Null Validation
projects.exampleOutput:
Dataset: [ 45, 88, 12, 95, 67, 34, 102, 78 ] (N = 8)

Calculated Statistics via Pointer Out-Parameters:
  • Minimum Value   : 12
  • Maximum Value   : 102
  • Total Sum       : 521
  • Average (Mean)  : 65.12
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Out-Parameters**: `int *minOut`, `int *maxOut`, `long long *sumOut`, `double *avgOut`.
2. **Dereferencing**: `*minOut = val` directly updates the caller's memory.
3. **Defensive Guard**: Returns early if any pointer argument is `NULL`.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `calculateArrayStatistics()`: Mutates 4 caller variables via pointer dereferencing.
2. Caller passes `&minVal`, `&maxVal`, etc.

projects.title: Banking Account State Machine with Persistent Static Transaction Ledger
projects.description: Global variables expose financial state to unintended mutations across an entire codebase. In this project, you will construct a Secure Banking Transaction Engine in C using static local variables. The transaction processor maintains an internal running vault balance and sequential transaction counter that persist across multiple invocations without exposing any mutable state to the global scope.
projects.learningOutcome: Static Local Variables, Data Encapsulation, State Persistence & Financial Ledger Invariants
projects.exampleText: Deposits and withdrawals across Swadeep, Tuhina, Abhronila, Debangshu
projects.exampleOutput:
[TXN-1001] Client: Swadeep      | Action: D | Amount: INR 25000.00
   >> Deposit Processed. Updated Vault Balance: INR 125000.00

[TXN-1002] Client: Tuhina       | Action: W | Amount: INR 15000.00
   >> Withdrawal Dispensed. Remaining Vault Balance: INR 110000.00

[TXN-1003] Client: Abhronila    | Action: W | Amount: INR 80000.00
   >> Withdrawal Dispensed. Remaining Vault Balance: INR 30000.00

[TXN-1004] Client: Debangshu    | Action: W | Amount: INR 50000.00
   >> REJECTED: Insufficient Vault Funds! Balance: INR 30000.00
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **static int sequence**: Increments on every invocation.
2. **static double vault**: Preserves current ledger balance.
3. **Encapsulation**: State is inaccessible outside `executeBankTransaction()`.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. Static variables allocated in the data segment.
2. Initialized once at startup.

projects.title: In-Place Array Reversal & Two-Pointer Element Transformation
projects.description: Manipulating buffers in-place without creating secondary heap allocations is essential for high-performance memory management. In this project, you will build an In-Place Array Reversal routine in C. The function accepts a pointer to an integer array and its length, swapping elements from the outside inward using two moving index pointers until they meet in the middle.
projects.learningOutcome: Array Pointer Passing, In-Place Memory Mutation, Two-Pointer Algorithm & const Array Read Safety
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Two Pointers**: `left = 0`, `right = size - 1`.
2. **Swap In-Place**: Swap `arr[left]` and `arr[right]` using temporary integer.
3. **Step**: `left++`, `right--` while `left < right`.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `reverseArrayInPlace()`: Directly mutates array memory without temporary array allocation.
2. `printArray()`: Qualified with `const int *arr` for read-only safety.

projects.title: Mathematical Recursion Suite: Factorial, GCD, and Binary Exponentiation
projects.description: Recursive decomposition allows complex mathematical series to be expressed with elegant, minimal code. In this project, you will build a Mathematical Recursion Toolkit in C. The suite includes: 1. Factorial computation (N!); 2. Euclidean Greatest Common Divisor (GCD); 3. Fast Binary Exponentiation (X^N in O(log N) time by halving exponents on even steps).
projects.learningOutcome: Base Cases, Recursive Step Invariants, Logarithmic Fast Power & Call Stack Expansion
projects.exampleOutput:
1. Recursive Factorial (6!)   : 720
2. Recursive GCD (252, 105)   : 21
3. Recursive Fast Power (2^10): 1024.00
4. Recursive Fast Power (3^5) : 243.00
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Factorial Base**: `if (n <= 1) return 1`.
2. **GCD Base**: `if (b == 0) return a; return recGCD(b, a % b)`.
3. **Fast Power**: `half = recFastPower(x, n/2); if (n%2==0) return half*half; else return x*half*half`.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. Encapsulates 3 classical recursive mathematical algorithms.
2. Demonstrates divide-and-conquer exponentiation.

projects.title: Tower of Hanoi 3-Peg Solver with Step Counting & State Ledger
projects.description: The Tower of Hanoi is the quintessential divide-and-conquer recursive puzzle. In this project, you will implement a 3-Peg Tower of Hanoi Solver in C. The recursive algorithm moves N-1 disks from Source to Auxiliary, moves the largest disk from Source to Destination, and moves the N-1 disks from Auxiliary to Destination. The program tracks the exact step sequence and updates a cumulative move counter via a pointer parameter.
projects.learningOutcome: Multi-Branch Divide-and-Conquer Recursion, State Ledger Tracking & 2^N - 1 Algorithmic Proof
projects.exampleOutput:
Solving Tower of Hanoi for N = 3 disks (Expected moves = 2^3 - 1 = 7):

  Step 01: Move disk 1 from Peg [A] -> Peg [C]
  Step 02: Move disk 2 from Peg [A] -> Peg [B]
  Step 03: Move disk 1 from Peg [C] -> Peg [B]
  Step 04: Move disk 3 from Peg [A] -> Peg [C]
  Step 05: Move disk 1 from Peg [B] -> Peg [A]
  Step 06: Move disk 2 from Peg [B] -> Peg [C]
  Step 07: Move disk 1 from Peg [A] -> Peg [C]

>> Total Disks Moved: 3 | Total Sequential Moves: 7
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Base Case**: If `disks == 1`, move disk 1 directly from `source` to `destination`.
2. **Step 1**: `solveHanoi(n-1, source, aux, dest)`.
3. **Step 2**: Move disk `n`.
4. **Step 3**: `solveHanoi(n-1, aux, dest, source)`.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `solveHanoi()`: Implements 3-peg recursive transfer.
2. `*moveCounter`: Tracks total executed moves.

projects.title: Recursive Palindrome & String Symmetry Verifier
projects.description: String symmetry verification can be solved recursively by comparing boundary characters and delegating the remaining inner substring to a smaller recursive call. In this project, you will build a Recursive String Palindrome Verifier in C. The function compares str[left] and str[right]; if they match, it recurses on (left + 1, right - 1) until the pointer indices meet or cross.
projects.learningOutcome: Recursive String Parsing, Boundary Pointer Comparison & Halting Invariants
projects.exampleOutput:
Word: radar           -> [PALINDROME]
Word: level           -> [PALINDROME]
Word: barrackpore     -> [NOT PALINDROME]
Word: rotator         -> [PALINDROME]
Word: computer        -> [NOT PALINDROME]
Word: madam           -> [PALINDROME]
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Base Case**: `if (left >= right) return true`.
2. **Mismatch**: `if (str[left] != str[right]) return false`.
3. **Recursive Step**: `return isPalindromeRecursive(str, left + 1, right - 1)`.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `checkStringPalindrome()`: Wrapper that computes length and invokes recursive helper.
2. `isPalindromeRecursive()`: Performs recursive boundary checks.

projects.title: Tail-Recursive Accumulator Engine vs Non-Tail Execution
projects.description: Non-tail recursive functions leave pending mathematical operations waiting on the stack, consuming O(N) stack memory. Tail-recursive functions pass the intermediate result forward in an accumulator parameter, enabling compilers with Tail Call Optimization (TCO) to reuse the current stack frame. In this project, you will implement and compare both non-tail and tail-recursive summation engines in C.
projects.learningOutcome: Tail Call Optimization (TCO), Accumulator Design Pattern & Stack Frame Reuse
projects.exampleOutput:
Sum from 1 to 100:
  • Non-Tail Recursive Result : 5050 (O(N) Stack Frames)
  • Tail-Recursive Result     : 5050 (O(1) Stack Frames under TCO)

>> Summary: Tail calls pass running totals in the accumulator argument,
   allowing compilers to reuse stack frames and prevent stack overflows!
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Non-Tail**: `return n + sumNonTail(n - 1)` (addition pending after return).
2. **Tail**: `return sumTail(n - 1, accumulator + n)` (recursive call is absolute last operation).
3. **Stack**: Tail calls convert to iterative jumps in optimized assembly.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `sumNonTail()`: Demonstrates standard recursive unwinding.
2. `sumTail()`: Uses accumulator for O(1) stack space optimization.

projects.title: Multi-Module Variable Linkage & Extern Configuration Router
projects.description: Professional C applications structure their architecture across multiple source files using internal and external linkage. In this project, you will build a System Configuration Router in C that models multi-file linkage. Global system state variables are declared with external linkage (extern), while private security daemon helpers are encapsulated using static internal linkage to prevent unauthorized global access.
projects.learningOutcome: External Linkage (extern), Internal Linkage (static functions), Information Hiding & Multi-File Architecture
projects.exampleOutput:
>> Executing Command 'INITIALIZE_NETWORK_BUFFER' under Security Profile 3

>> Executing Command 'CALIBRATE_TELEMETRY_SENSORS' under Security Profile 3

>> Executing Command 'FLUSH_STORAGE_JOURNAL' under Security Profile 5
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **extern variables**: Visible to all compilation units linked in the final executable.
2. **static functions**: Hidden from the linker; callable only within the local file.
3. **Encapsulation**: Prevents symbol name collisions across large libraries.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `g_securityLevel`: Global variable with external linkage.
2. `logInternalSecurityCheck()`: File-private static helper function.

projects.title: Recursive Fibonacci Memoization Cache with Static Lookup Array
projects.description: Naive recursive Fibonacci runs in exponential O(2^N) time due to massive overlapping subproblem re-evaluations. In this project, you will construct a Memoized Recursive Fibonacci Accelerator in C. Using a static cache array inside the recursive function, computed terms are saved upon first calculation. Subsequent calls return cached results in instantaneous O(1) time, reducing total time complexity from O(2^N) to O(N).
projects.learningOutcome: Memoization Caching, Dynamic Programming Intuition & Static Persistent Lookup Arrays
projects.exampleOutput:
Computing Fibonacci terms with O(N) Memoization Cache:

  • Fibonacci( 0) = 0
  • Fibonacci( 2) = 1
  • Fibonacci( 4) = 3
  • Fibonacci( 6) = 8
  • Fibonacci( 8) = 21
  • Fibonacci(10) = 55
  • Fibonacci(20) = 6765
  • Fibonacci(50) = 12586269025 (Instantaneous via static cache!)
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Static Cache**: `static unsigned long long memo[90]` persists across calls.
2. **Cache Check**: `if (memo[n] != 0) return memo[n]`.
3. **Store & Return**: `memo[n] = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2); return memo[n]`.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `fibonacciMemoized()`: Implements top-down dynamic memoization.
2. Computes 50th Fibonacci term instantaneously without recursion timeouts.

projects.title: Pass-by-Const-Pointer High-Performance Student Record Manager
projects.description: Passing large structure objects by value copies entire memory blocks onto the call stack, wasting CPU cycles. Passing structures via const pointers passes only an 8-byte RAM address while guaranteeing that the function cannot accidentally modify caller data. In this project, you will build a Student Academic Record Manager in C that inspects transcript records using const struct pointers and arrow operators (->).
projects.learningOutcome: Const Struct Pointers (const Struct*), Arrow Operator (->), Read-Only Invariants & Memory Performance
projects.exampleText: Student 1: Swadeep Sharma (GPA 3.85) | Student 2: Tuhina Mukherjee (GPA 3.92)
projects.exampleOutput:
TRANSCRIPT: Roll #101 | Name: Swadeep Sharma
  Scores: Physics = 88.0, Chemistry = 92.5, Math = 95.0
  Overall Calculated GPA: 3.85 / 4.00 | Status: IN GOOD STANDING

TRANSCRIPT: Roll #102 | Name: Tuhina Mukherjee
  Scores: Physics = 94.0, Chemistry = 89.0, Math = 96.5
  Overall Calculated GPA: 3.92 / 4.00 | Status: IN GOOD STANDING
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Pass by Pointer**: `const StudentRecord *student` passes an 8-byte address.
2. **Read-Only Safety**: `const` qualifier prevents any modifications to fields.
3. **Arrow Operator**: `student->gpa` dereferences and accesses struct members.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `printStudentTranscript()`: High-speed read-only struct printer.
2. Eliminates struct memory duplication on the call stack.

projects.title: Recursive Sum of Digits & Digital Root Reducer
projects.description: The Digital Root of a number is the single digit obtained by repeatedly summing its digits until a single-digit integer remains. In this project, you will construct a Recursive Digital Root Reducer in C. First, a recursive function computes the sum of digits by peeling (n % 10) and recursing on (n / 10). Second, a digital root function repeatedly delegates to the digit sum routine until the value is less than 10.
projects.learningOutcome: Digit Peeling Recursion, Nested Function Delegation & Mathematical Base Cases
projects.exampleOutput:
Number: 12345      -> Sum of Digits = 15 -> Digital Root = 6
Number: 98765      -> Sum of Digits = 35 -> Digital Root = 8
Number: 493193     -> Sum of Digits = 29 -> Digital Root = 2
Number: 2026       -> Sum of Digits = 10 -> Digital Root = 1
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Digit Sum**: `if (n == 0) return 0; return (n % 10) + sumOfDigits(n / 10)`.
2. **Digital Root**: `if (n < 10) return n; return digitalRoot(sumOfDigits(n))`.
3. **Halting Invariant**: Digit sum strictly reduces positive integers.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `sumOfDigitsRecursive()`: Extracts digits via modulo and integer division.
2. `digitalRootRecursive()`: Reduces multi-digit sums to a single digit.

projects.title: Register Storage Class Micro-Benchmark for Iteration Loops
projects.description: The register storage class requests that the compiler store frequently accessed local variables inside high-speed CPU registers rather than system RAM. In this project, you will build a Register Calculation Micro-Benchmark in C. The program executes iterative accumulation loops using register variables and explores the architectural restriction prohibiting the use of address-of operators (&) on register variables.
projects.learningOutcome: Register Storage Class (register), CPU Register Hardware vs RAM & Silicon Level Optimization
projects.exampleOutput:
Executing calculation loop for 10000 iterations using CPU register variables...
>> Result calculated in registers: 149995000

Executing calculation loop for 50000 iterations using CPU register variables...
>> Result calculated in registers: 3749975000
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **register specifier**: Requests CPU register storage (e.g. EAX, EBX, R8).
2. **Speed**: Eliminates memory load/store bus cycles for fast loop counters.
3. **Address Restriction**: `&regVar` is illegal because registers have no memory addresses.
projects.codeExplanation: 1. `performRegisterLoopCalculation()`: Executes accumulator loop using register variables.

projects.title: Mutual Indirect Recursion Parser
projects.description: Mutual (Indirect) Recursion occurs when function A calls function B, and function B in turn calls function A. In this project, you will implement a Mutual Recursion Even/Odd Number Classifier in C. The function isEven(n) checks if n == 0 (true) or delegates to isOdd(n - 1); similarly, isOdd(n) checks if n == 0 (false) or delegates to isEven(n - 1). You will use forward function declarations (prototypes) to resolve mutual compiler dependencies.
projects.learningOutcome: Mutual Indirect Recursion, Forward Function Prototypes & Cyclic Call Stack Traversal
projects.exampleOutput:
Number:  0 -> isEven = TRUE  | isOdd = FALSE
Number:  1 -> isEven = FALSE | isOdd = TRUE 
Number:  4 -> isEven = TRUE  | isOdd = FALSE
Number:  7 -> isEven = FALSE | isOdd = TRUE 
Number: 12 -> isEven = TRUE  | isOdd = FALSE
Number: 19 -> isEven = FALSE | isOdd = TRUE 
Number: 42 -> isEven = TRUE  | isOdd = FALSE
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Forward Declaration**: `bool isOddMutual(int n);` declared before `isEvenMutual()`.
2. **isEven(n)**: `if (n == 0) return true; return isOdd(n - 1)`.
3. **isOdd(n)**: `if (n == 0) return false; return isEven(n - 1)`.
projects.codeExplanation:
1. Forward prototypes enable mutual compilation.
2. Demonstrates indirect cyclic recursion.

projects.title: Recursive Decimal to Binary / Hexadecimal Base Converter
projects.description: Converting numbers from decimal to binary or hexadecimal generates digits in reverse order (least significant digit first). By using recursion and printing the modulo remainder during the unwinding phase (after the recursive call returns), the digits naturally print in correct left-to-right positional order without needing extra string reversal buffers. In this project, you will construct a Recursive Number Base Converter in C.
projects.learningOutcome: Stack Unwinding Execution Order, Base Conversion (Binary / Hex) & Bufferless Number Printing
projects.exampleOutput:
Decimal: 5     | Binary: 101 | Hexadecimal: 0x5
Decimal: 29    | Binary: 11101 | Hexadecimal: 0x1D
Decimal: 255   | Binary: 11111111 | Hexadecimal: 0xFF
Decimal: 1024  | Binary: 10000000000 | Hexadecimal: 0x400
Decimal: 65535 | Binary: 1111111111111111 | Hexadecimal: 0xFFFF
projects.logicExplanation:
1. **Recurse First**: `if (n > 1) printBinaryRecursive(n / 2)`.
2. **Print on Unwind**: `printf("%d", n % 2)`.
3. **Natural Reversal**: Deepest calls return first, printing the most significant digit first!
projects.codeExplanation:
1. `printBinaryRecursive()`: Recursively extracts binary bits.
2. `printHexRecursive()`: Recursively formats hexadecimal digits.
